title: "To have" in Hebrew: יֵשׁ לִי
topic: יֵשׁ לִי / אֵין לִי; ל־ with pronouns (לִי, לְךָ, לָךְ…)
why: In Hebrew, "to have" is expressed with יֵשׁ (there is) and the preposition לְ: this lesson teaches you "I have, I don't have" and all the forms לִי, לְךָ, לָךְ… It opens the unit "Everyday life," right after the present tense, with everyday objects and pets.

No verb \"to have\"

Hebrew has no verb \"to have.\" To say \"I have,\" it takes יֵשׁ (there is), which you already know, and adds לִי (to me): literally, \"there is to me.\"

יֵשׁ לִי כֶּלֶב.I have a dog. [yesh li kelev]

For the negative, יֵשׁ becomes אֵין (there isn't):

אֵין לִי מְכוֹנִית.I don't have a car. [ein li mekhonit]

Watch out: there's no \"don't,\" no \"a\" and no \"any.\" You simply say \"there isn't to me car.\" And never לֹא יֵשׁ: the negative of יֵשׁ is always אֵין.

A question is asked with intonation alone: יֵשׁ לְךָ כֶּלֶב? — כֵּן, יֵשׁ לִי. / לֹא, אֵין לִי.

", "

לְ with pronouns: לִי, לְךָ, לָךְ…

The preposition לְ (to) fuses with the pronoun and takes an ending. Just as with \"you,\" there is one form for a man and one for a woman.

HebrewPronunciationMeaning
לִיlito me
לְךָlekhato you (to a man)
לָךְlakhto you (to a woman)
לוֹloto him
לָהּlato her
לָנוּlanuto us
לָכֶםlakhemto you, plural (men or a mixed group)
לָכֶןlakhento you, plural (women)
לָהֶםlahemto them (m.)
לָהֶןlahento them (f.)

Trap: לוֹ (to him) and לֹא (no) are both pronounced \"lo.\" In speech, the meaning decides; in writing, look at the last letter.

לֹא, אֵין לוֹ זְמַן.No, he doesn't have time. [lo, ein lo zman]

Before a name, לְ is attached too: לְנֹעָה יֵשׁ חָתוּל. (Noa has a cat.) The final ה of לָהּ has a dot (the mappiq): it doesn't change the sound, \"la.\"

", "

My things, my pets

What you own doesn't change יֵשׁ at all: it stays the same for masculine, feminine and plural. Only the adjective agrees, with the object.

יֵשׁ לָהּ מְכוֹנִית חֲדָשָׁה.She has a new car. [yesh la mekhonit khadasha]
יֵשׁ לָנוּ כֶּלֶב גָּדוֹל וַחֲתוּלָה קְטַנָּה.We have a big dog and a little female cat. [yesh lanu kelev gadol va-khatula ktana]

Two everyday expressions: אֵין לִי זְמַן (I don't have time) and אֵין בְּעָיָה (no problem: here without לְ, \"there's no problem\").

Without לְ, יֵשׁ means \"there is\": יֵשׁ חָתוּל בַּבַּיִת (there's a cat in the house). With לְ, it means \"to have\": יֵשׁ לִי חָתוּל (I have a cat).
